lead: A mismatched load reflects power. A quarter-wave transformer inserts a line section one quarter wavelength long whose characteristic impedance is the geometric mean of the source and load impedances, so a real load looks like the source at the design frequency and, for the ideal section, at odd harmonics. A stub matching network instead adds a short piece of open or shorted line at a chosen distance; it cancels the load reactance and leaves the input impedance equal to Z0. These two methods are the standard hand calculations for matching lines, and they appear in RF boards, antenna feeds and test setups.
prereq: You need: 1.1 for Z0 and wavelength, 1.2 for reflection, and 1.3 for input impedance of loaded and open/short lines.

blocks.text: Take a lossless line of characteristic impedance Z0 feeding a real load ZL. Insert a section of length l and characteristic impedance Z0′ between them. The input impedance of a loaded line is Zin = Z0′ (ZL + jZ0′ tan βl)/(Z0′ + jZL tan βl), where β = 2π/λ is the phase constant and λ is the wavelength in the section. At l = λ/4, βl = π/2 and tan βl tends to infinity, so Zin → Z0′²/ZL.

Set Zin = Z0: Z0′²/ZL = Z0, so Z0′ = √(Z0 ZL). Z0′ is the geometric mean of source and load. For 50 Ω and 100 Ω, Z0′ = 70.71 Ω. The section is exactly λ/4 at the design frequency f0, with λ = vp/f0; vp is the phase velocity in the section, not c unless the dielectric is air.

blocks.where: Z0 is the source-line impedance in Ω; ZL is the real load resistance in Ω; Z0′ is the quarter-wave section impedance in Ω; vp is the phase velocity in m/s; f0 is the design frequency in Hz; l is the section length in m.

blocks.text: The match is exact at f0, and also at odd multiples 3f0, 5f0, ... for the ideal lossless section, because βl = π/2, 3π/2, 5π/2, ... there. Around f0, excluding those odd-harmonic points, the electrical length is not 90°, tan βl is finite, and Zin moves away from Z0. The useful matching band around f0 is therefore narrow, and the bandwidth shrinks as ZL/Z0 departs from 1. It is used at antenna feeds, between a 50 Ω cable and a 100 Ω printed dipole, and in single-frequency RF paths. Some syllabi call this a quarter-wave matching section.

A stub is a short piece of line connected in shunt (across the line) or in series (in the line). It adds pure susceptance or reactance. Use a shunt stub when the load admittance can be adjusted; use a series stub when impedance is more convenient. The design has two unknowns: distance d from the load to the stub, and stub length l_s.

For a shunt stub, work in admittance. Move along the line from the load until the input admittance has real part equal to Y0 = 1/Z0. At that plane write Y(d) = Y0 + jB(d). A stub of input admittance Ys = jBs is connected in parallel, so the total admittance is Y0 + j[B(d) + Bs]. Choose Bs = −B(d). The line then sees admittance Y0, corresponding to impedance Z0.

The stub susceptance depends on its termination. A shorted stub of characteristic admittance Y0s = 1/Z0s has Ys = −jY0s cot βl_s. An open stub has Ys = jY0s tan βl_s. Set either expression equal to −B(d) and solve for l_s. A series stub is the dual: move until Z(d) = Z0 + jX(d), then choose a stub reactance Xs = −X(d). A shorted series stub gives Zs = jZ0s tan βl_s; an open series stub gives Zs = −jZ0s cot βl_s.

items: Normalize the load admittance to Y0.
Find the distance d (from the load toward the generator) where Re[Y(d)] = Y0. There are generally two possible stub positions within λ/2; choose the practical one.
Compute the susceptance B(d) at that plane.
Choose open or short stub and solve for length l_s so that Bs = −B(d).
Check that the input admittance is Y0 + j0.

blocks.text: The distance d is measured from the load, not from the source. The stub length l_s is measured from the junction to the open or short end. In microstrip, an open stub is a printed line with no via; a short stub needs a via to ground. The stub adds no loss in the ideal model, but real stubs have conductor and dielectric loss.

Matching is specified over a band, not at one point. A common criterion is |Γ| ≤ 0.2, which gives VSWR ≤ 1.5. The quarter-wave transformer meets this over a limited band. For ZL/Z0 = 2 and |Γ| ≤ 0.2 (VSWR ≤ 1.5), an ideal single-section transformer has roughly 78% bandwidth, from about 0.61f0 to 1.39f0. Larger impedance ratios or tighter VSWR reduce the bandwidth.

Stub matching can be adjusted for wider bandwidth by choosing the stub location that gives the smallest slope of input admittance with frequency, and by using a stub with the required susceptance at a length away from resonance. In practice, CAD optimization sweeps d and l_s to minimize the maximum |Γ| over the band.

Design criteria are: match within the specified VSWR over the band; keep characteristic impedances realizable (about 20 Ω to 120 Ω in microstrip); keep stub lengths short enough to avoid high loss and unwanted radiation; and choose open or short stubs from fabrication constraints. Multi-section quarter-wave transformers and tapered lines trade length for bandwidth; filter design is in Unit 4, Microwave Components, Devices and Measurements. Graphical solution is in 1.5; printed-line realization is in 1.6.

figure.caption: A 50 Ω source feeds a quarter-wave section of 70.71 Ω into a 100 Ω real load; with vp = 2×10⁸ m/s, at 2.4 GHz the section is 2.08 cm long. The useful match is narrow around the design frequency; the ideal section also matches exactly at odd harmonics.

spec.title: Quarter-wave transformer
spec.aria: A 50 Ω source feeds a quarter-wave section of 70.71 Ω, which matches a 100 Ω real load.

examples.question: A 100 Ω resistive load is to be matched to a 50 Ω line at 2.4 GHz using a quarter-wave transformer. The phase velocity in the section is vp = 2×10⁸ m/s. Find Z0′ and the physical length of the section.
steps: The load is real, so the quarter-wave transformer formula applies: Z0′ = √(Z0 ZL) = √(50×100) = √5000 = 70.71 Ω.
The wavelength in the section is λ = vp/f0 = (2×10⁸ m/s)/(2.4×10⁹ Hz) = 0.08333 m = 8.33 cm.
The quarter-wave length is l = λ/4 = 8.33 cm/4 = 2.08 cm.
examples.answer: Z0′ = 70.71 Ω and the section length is l = 2.08 cm at 2.4 GHz.
examples.check:
import math
Z0 = 50.0
ZL = 100.0
f = 2.4e9
vp = 2.0e8
Zp = math.sqrt(Z0*ZL)
lam = vp/f
l = lam/4
print(f'{Zp:.2f}')
print(f'{lam*100:.2f}')
print(f'{l*100:.2f}')

traps: Using a quarter-wave transformer directly on a complex load: the reactance must be cancelled first (for example with a stub, or a length of line that makes the impedance real), or use a different matching network.
Measuring the stub distance d from the source instead of from the load.
Using c/f for wavelength in a line: use vp/f, where vp is set by the dielectric.
Confusing stub position d with stub length l_s; l_s is measured from the junction to the open or short end.
Assuming the match holds over a wide band: a single quarter-wave section is narrowband.

quiz.q: State the characteristic impedance of a quarter-wave transformer that matches a real load ZL to a line Z0.
Why does a λ/4 section invert the load impedance as Z0′²/ZL?
quiz.a: At l = λ/4, βl = π/2, so tan βl tends to infinity in the input-impedance formula. The ZL term dominates the denominator and the result becomes Z0′²/ZL.

quiz.q: Match a 200 Ω resistive load to a 50 Ω line at one frequency with a quarter-wave transformer. Find Z0′.
At the chosen shunt-stub plane, Y(d) = 0.02 + j0.01 S and Y0 = 0.02 S. What stub susceptance Bs is needed?
quiz.a: The stub must cancel the imaginary part: Bs = −0.01 S.

quiz.q: Why is a quarter-wave transformer not used directly on a complex load?
quiz.a: The load reactance makes Zin complex after the λ/4 section, so the input is not equal to Z0. The reactance must be cancelled first with a stub or a complex matching design.

quiz.q: Why does the bandwidth of a single-section quarter-wave transformer shrink as ZL/Z0 increases?
quiz.a: The section is fixed at λ/4 only at f0. Away from f0 the electrical length changes, and a larger impedance ratio produces a larger reflection for the same length error. The tolerance band therefore becomes narrower.

quiz.q: From where are d and l_s measured in single-stub matching?
quiz.a: d is measured from the load toward the generator; l_s is measured from the stub junction to the open or short end.

beyond: Not for the exam. Multi-section quarter-wave transformers use binomial or Chebyshev impedance steps to widen bandwidth. Tapered transmission lines change impedance continuously along the line. CAD tools optimize stub positions and lengths with real component models and layout parasitics. Search for 'multi-section impedance transformer', 'tapered line matching' and 'single stub matching microstrip'.
